youtube.title: C++ std::vector: The Array That Grows | C++ Programming EP 35
youtube.description: In this episode you will make a vector and add items with push_back, read the size and the items and loop over a vector, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 std::vector · 1:22 Grow a vector · 2:16 A vector in memory · 3:03 Second program · 4:18 Recap · 4:48 Bug of the Day · 5:44 Challenge · 6:08 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet the most useful container in C plus plus. A vector grows when you add items.

scenes.onScreen: "std::vector": numbered lines (1. A vector grows and shrinks; 2. push_back adds an item at the end; 3. It manages its own memory) and an analogy card: a stretchy bag: it grows when you add more shopping
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A vector is an array that can grow and shrink. Push back adds an item at the end. The size function tells you how many items it holds. A vector looks after its own memory. You never write new or delete. Think of a stretchy shopping bag. It grows when you add more shopping. Vector is the most used container in C plus plus. When you do not know how many items you need, use a vector. Inside, a vector keeps a plain array. When the array is full, it makes a bigger one, copies the items, and drops the old one. You never see this work, but it is why adding at the end is fast.
points: push_back adds an item at the end

analogy.title: std::vector

scenes.onScreen: vec.cpp: push_back adds items one by one
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 2] The vector header gives us the vector type. [HL 6] The type goes in angle brackets. This vector is empty. [HL 7] Push back adds ten at the end. [HL 9] Two more pushes add twenty and thirty. [HL 10] The size is three. [HL 11] Index one is twenty. [HL 6] The type in angle brackets says what the vector holds. A new vector starts empty. [HL 7] Push back adds one item at the end. [HL 8] The next item goes after it. [HL 9] And the next. [HL 10] The size is now three. [HL 11] You read an item with square brackets, as with an array. Index one is twenty.

scenes.onScreen: the vector object on the stack points to its items on the heap
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: The vector has two parts. The small vector object lives on the stack. The items live on the heap. The object points to the first item. When you push back more items, the vector asks for a bigger block and moves the items. Notice the difference from an array. The array has a fixed size. The vector has a size and a capacity. The capacity is how many items fit before the next growth. It is usually bigger than the size.

scenes.onScreen: veclist.cpp: a vector made from a list, then a loop
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] A vector can start with a list of values. [HL 7] Push back adds sixteen at the end. [HL 8] A range-based for visits every item. [HL 12] Back gives the last item, which is sixteen. [HL 13] Pop back removes the last item. [HL 14] Now the size is three. [HL 6] You can start a vector with a list of values. [HL 7] Push back adds sixteen at the end. [HL 12] The back function gives the last item. [HL 13] Pop back removes it. [HL 14] The size is then three again.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as veclist dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints the four numbers, then sixteen, then three. Notice the numbers. The loop prints four, eight, fifteen and sixteen. Then the back call prints sixteen. After the pop, the size is three.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A vector grows and shrinks. Two. Push back adds an item at the end. Three. Size tells you how many items it holds. Four. A vector looks after its own memory. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Push back adds an item at the end.
Size tells you how many items it holds.
A vector looks after its own memory.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A missing vector header
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The program uses vector, but there is no include line for it. The compiler says vector was not declared in this scope. It suggests the header in a note. Add the include line for vector at the top. The vector type lives in its own header. Without the include line, the compiler does not know the word vector. The error says that vector is not declared. Add the include line at the top, and the error goes away.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

vec.cpp: In function 'int main()':
vec.cpp:5:5: error: 'vector' was not declared in this scope
    5 |     vector<int> v;
      |     ^~~~~~
vec.cpp:2:1: note: 'std::vector' is defined in header '<vector>'; did you forget to '#include <vector>'?
    1 | #include <iostream>
bug.why: The vector type lives in its own header. Without the include line, the compiler has never heard of vector.

pun: "My vector told me it needs space. I said, you can grow, I believe in you."
challenge: Use a vector. Push back the numbers from one to five, then print their sum. Hint: add the numbers to the sum in a loop, after you fill the vector.
challengeAnswer: Use a for loop with push back for each number. Then use a range-based for to add them. The sum is fifteen.
